case_analysis.focal_point: Whether ERISA/MPPAA permits a multiemployer pension plan to recalculate and increase an employer’s withdrawal liability by retroactively changing the actuarial assumptions (especially the interest rate) used to compute the original assessment.
case_analysis.legal_provision: ERISA as amended by the Multiemployer Pension Plan Amendments Act of 1980 (MPPAA), principally the withdrawal-liability provisions governing calculation, notice/assessment, and actuarial assumptions (e.g., 29 U.S.C. §§ 1381–1399, including the requirements that assumptions be actuarially reasonable and applied in determining unfunded vested benefits).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that once a plan issues a withdrawal-liability assessment using a particular set of actuarial assumptions, ERISA/MPPAA does not allow the plan to later revise that assessment by retroactively substituting new assumptions (notably a different interest-rate assumption) to generate a higher number. They contend that allowing retroactive changes undermines predictability and finality in withdrawal liability, invites manipulation, and conflicts with the Second Circuit’s decision in Metz, which they characterize as barring the precise practice at issue. In their view, any correction should be limited to true clerical/arithmetical errors, not a discretionary re-selection of key assumptions after the fact that materially changes liability by millions of dollars.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (supported by the AFL-CIO, Pension Rights Center, and the United States/PBGC) argues that MPPAA’s text and structure focus on accurate measurement of unfunded vested benefits using actuarially reasonable assumptions, and do not freeze a plan into an initial assumption set if later determined to be incorrect or inconsistent with actuarial standards. They contend that permitting recalculation to reflect proper assumptions is consistent with protecting plan participants and the insurance system, prevents under-collection that would shift costs to remaining employers or jeopardize benefits, and fits within the statutory regime that channels disputes into arbitration with deference to plan actuaries’ determinations. They also dispute petitioners’ reading of Metz (and/or argue it is distinguishable), emphasizing that plans must be able to correct assumptions to ensure withdrawal liability reflects statutory reality rather than a mistaken initial calculation.
key_precedents: Jacobson v. Fireman’s Fund Ins. Co., 111 F.3d (2d Cir. 1997)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito press the strongest counter: §§ 1393 and 1401(a)(3)(B), as Concrete Pipe describes, prioritize actuarial reasonableness enforced through arbitration, not any express “one-shot” finality rule. But that accuracy-through-arbitration framework presupposes a determinate § 1399(b)(1) notice-and-demand that starts fixed, short employer windows for review and arbitration; allowing a sponsor to later reselect a discretionary, outcome-driving assumption (like the interest rate) and issue a materially higher redetermination would destabilize those statutory deadlines and turn the pay-now-dispute-later regime into a moving target without clear textual authorization. Concrete Pipe informs how the initial determination is reviewed (presumption and arbitral correction), not an implied power to reset the determination itself after notice; § 1391’s snapshot valuation reinforces that the relevant contest is over the reasonableness of the sponsor’s timely demand as of the measurement date. I therefore remain with the narrow line Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh articulate: permit clerical/arithmetical or clear application corrections, but not post-notice discretionary assumption swaps that increase liability.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s “moving target” argument identifies a real structural concern about deadlines in §§ 1399(b) and 1401(a), but structure cannot supply a categorical irrevocability rule Congress did not enact. Section 1401(a)(3)(B) expressly contemplates that the sponsor’s determinations—including assumptions—may be displaced in arbitration upon a showing of “unreasonable” assumptions or “significant error,” and Concrete Pipe confirms Congress chose accuracy-through-arbitration with a rebuttable presumption, not finality-through-freeze. Justice Roberts’s proposed line (clerical errors yes; assumption swaps no) is administrability-driven rather than text-driven, and it risks entrenching an assessment that is materially noncompliant with § 1393’s reasonableness mandate merely because it was first-in-time. The better reading is that any revision must remain tied to the same measurement date and remain fully subject to the statute’s review/arbitration protections, rather than being barred outright when the error goes to an actuarial assumption.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The strongest point from the other side is Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s structural “moving target” argument: §§ 1399(b) and 1401(a) operate with short, sequential deadlines that work best when the plan issues a stable notice-and-demand. But structure cannot supply an unstated irrevocability rule for core actuarial inputs when § 1401(a)(3)(B) expressly contemplates correcting determinations infected by “unreasonable” assumptions or “significant error,” and Concrete Pipe (as Justice Thomas notes) describes Congress’s choice to police accuracy through arbitration rather than freeze the first number issued. Metz, invoked by Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Barrett, can be read to prevent opportunistic repricing, but it does not justify a bright-line bar that would entrench a materially unreasonable interest-rate assumption and shift costs to remaining employers—precisely what § 1393’s aggregate reasonableness mandate is designed to prevent. Administrability concerns can be addressed by tying any revision to the same measurement date and preserving the employer’s review/arbitration rights, not by reading into the statute a categorical prohibition Congress did not enact.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s “moving target” finality concern is the Petitioners’ strongest point, because §§ 1399(b) and 1401(a) do run on short, sequenced deadlines that can be undermined by serial, self-serving re-demands. But their proposed irrevocability rule still lacks a textual anchor: § 1401(a)(3)(B) expressly contemplates correction of “unreasonable” assumptions and “significant error,” and as Justice Thomas stresses (consistent with Concrete Pipe) Congress chose accuracy policed through arbitration rather than a categorical freeze keyed to the first notice. Metz usefully warns against opportunistic repricing, yet under a pragmatic reading it should operate as an abuse/motive constraint and a same-measurement-date requirement—not as a bright-line bar that entrenches materially noncompliant assumptions, shifts shortfalls to other employers, and ultimately threatens participants’ benefits. Administrability can be protected without sacrificing statutory compliance by requiring prompt corrected notice tied to the original measurement date and preserving the employer’s full arbitration rights, rather than prohibiting correction of serious actuarial mistakes altogether.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point—that § 1401(a)(3)(B)’s rebuttable presumption for “unreasonable” assumptions or “significant error,” as Concrete Pipe describes, favors accuracy over finality—does not supply an affirmative textual grant to the sponsor to issue a second, higher § 1399(b)(1) “notice and demand” by reselecting a discretionary, outcome-driving assumption after the statutory process has been triggered. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, the statute’s sequenced, short, deadline-driven review/arbitration architecture presupposes a determinate demand that anchors the employer’s pay-now-dispute-later obligations; reading an implied, iterative revision power into §§ 1393/1401 would destabilize that design without clear textual footing. Concrete Pipe affects my analysis only by confirming the deference/arbitration channel for testing the reasonableness of the sponsor’s initial determination—not by authorizing serial re-demands that effectively reset the clock. I remain persuaded the best reconciliation is a narrow correction window for clerical/arithmetic or clear application mistakes, while disputes about actuarial reasonableness of core assumptions belong in arbitration keyed to the original demand.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s best point is textual: § 1401(a)(3)(B) and Concrete Pipe contemplate a presumption of correctness rebuttable in arbitration for “unreasonable” assumptions or “significant error,” and nothing expressly says the first demand is irrevocable. But that presumption-and-arbitration regime is triggered by a specific statutory event—§ 1399(b)(1)’s “notice and demand” issued “as soon as practicable”—which in turn starts short, mandatory employer deadlines in §§ 1399(b)(2) and 1401(a); reading an implied power to later reselect a core, discretionary assumption and retroactively increase liability makes those deadlines—and the pay-now-dispute-later architecture—textually incoherent. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Concrete Pipe describes how to review the sponsor’s initial determination within the statutory process; it does not supply a freestanding reopening authority Congress did not provide. I remain persuaded the best textual-original public meaning is a narrow correction power for clerical/arithmetic or clear application mistakes, not post-notice assumption swaps that materially change the liability target.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s textual argument from §§ 1393 and 1401(a)(3)(B), reinforced by Concrete Pipe, is the strongest point for Respondent, but I read those provisions as defining the standard and forum for testing the sponsor’s initial § 1399(b)(1) determination—not as granting an implied, unilateral power to issue a materially higher second demand by reselecting a core actuarial assumption after notice. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, the statute’s sequenced, deadline-driven architecture (employer review and arbitration windows keyed to the notice) presupposes a determinate anchor; allowing discretionary post-notice assumption swaps makes liability a moving target and undercuts the pay-now-dispute-later regime Congress chose. Justice Alito’s solvency concern is real, but Congress addressed that through timely, accurate initial demands and arbitration to correct “unreasonable” assumptions or “significant error,” not by enabling iterative, sponsor-controlled recalculation that effectively resets statutory deadlines. I therefore remain with the narrow administrable line Roberts proposes: clerical/arithmetical or clear application corrections are permissible, but discretionary post-notice reselection of key assumptions that increases liability is not.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest textual point is that § 1401(a)(3)(B) makes the sponsor’s determination only presumptively correct and expressly rebuttable for “unreasonable” assumptions or “significant error,” which—along with Concrete Pipe—confirms Congress’s preference for arbitral review of actuarial judgments. But that speaks to how the initial § 1399(b)(1) determination is reviewed within the statutory process; it does not supply an affirmative, unilateral power to issue a second, higher “notice and demand” after the employer’s fixed review/arbitration clocks have begun to run, a structural feature Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan rightly emphasize as central to § 1399(b)(2) and § 1401(a). Section 1391’s measurement-date rule is best read, in original public meaning, as a snapshot anchoring both valuation inputs and the procedural sequence, leaving room for clerical/arithmetic/application corrections but not for post-notice reselection of a core discretionary assumption that materially increases liability. Because the respondent’s position requires implying a reopening mechanism that the enacted text does not provide and that destabilizes the statute’s deadline-driven architecture, I remain with petitioner.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Sotomayor press the strongest point: § 1401(a)(3)(B) and Concrete Pipe contemplate correction of “unreasonable” assumptions and “significant error,” and they argue that nothing in §§ 1399 or 1401 makes the first demand irrevocable. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, that rebuttable-presumption/arbitration framework is embedded in a deadline-driven procedural architecture—§ 1399(b)’s notice-and-demand triggers short review/arbitration windows and a pay-now-dispute-later regime—that depends on a stable, determinate assessment; allowing unilateral post-notice reselection of a core, discretionary, outcome-driving assumption effectively converts Congress’s process into a sponsor-controlled moving target. Concrete Pipe, on my reading, speaks to deference and the arbitral mechanism for testing the reasonableness of the sponsor’s initial determination, not to an affirmative power to retroactively revise the baseline in a way that increases liability and undermines procedural fairness. A pragmatic, procedurally fair reconciliation is to allow correction of genuine clerical/arithmetic/application mistakes, while channeling disputes about the reasonableness of initial assumptions into the existing review/arbitration process keyed to the original notice.

John Roberts.reasoning: MPPAA’s withdrawal-liability scheme fixes the calculation of unfunded vested benefits “as of the end of the plan year preceding the plan year in which the employer withdraws,” 29 U.S.C. § 1391(b)(2)(E)(i), and then requires prompt notice and a tightly channeled review/arbitration process, §§ 1399(b), 1401(a), which presuppose a determinate assessment rather than a moving target. Allowing a plan to retroactively swap in new actuarial assumptions (especially the interest rate) after issuing its assessment would undermine finality and predictability in that notice/arbitration structure and invite strategic “re-pricing” rather than correction of genuine clerical errors. The Second Circuit’s rule in Metz—requiring actuarial assumptions to be those adopted as of the measurement date—best fits the statute’s emphasis on a fixed measurement date and supports institutional legitimacy by enforcing a clear, administrable limit while still leaving plans room to defend the reasonableness of the assumptions they timely selected. A narrow holding recognizing only limited corrections (e.g., arithmetical/clerical mistakes) would respect precedent and the statutory design without destabilizing the multiemployer system.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The MPPAA’s text directs that withdrawal liability be determined using “actuarial assumptions and methods” that are “in the aggregate, reasonable,” and it establishes a mandatory arbitration mechanism to test whether the plan’s determination rests on unreasonable assumptions or a significant application error. See 29 U.S.C. §§ 1391, 1399, 1401(a)(1), 1401(a)(3)(B). Nothing in § 1399’s notice-and-demand provisions freezes a plan irrevocably to its first set of assumptions; rather, Congress provided for correction through arbitration and judicial review so that liability reflects the statute’s required actuarial reality. Concrete Pipe & Prods. v. Constr. Laborers Pension Tr., 508 U.S. 602 (1993), confirms that actuarial determinations are presumptively correct but rebuttable under § 1401(a)(3)(B), which is consistent with allowing recalculation when the original assumptions prove inconsistent with the statutory standard.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: MPPAA’s text makes the employer’s obligation turn on an accurate determination of the plan’s “unfunded vested benefits” using actuarial assumptions and methods that are “in the aggregate, reasonable.” 29 U.S.C. §§ 1381, 1391, 1401(a)(3)(B). Nothing in §§ 1381–1399 clearly “freezes” an initial interest-rate assumption if the plan later concludes the original assumption was unreasonable or misapplied; instead, the statute channels disputes into arbitration and affords presumptive correctness to the sponsor’s determinations unless the employer proves unreasonableness or significant error. Concrete Pipe confirms this framework—presuming actuarial determinations correct subject to the statutory reasonableness/“significant error” showing—and it would have serious practical consequences for plan solvency and remaining employers if plans were barred from correcting materially mistaken assumptions that understate liability. Metz, to the extent it suggests a stricter finality rule, cannot override the statute’s emphasis on actuarial reasonableness and the arbitration scheme Congress chose.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: MPPAA’s withdrawal-liability scheme is aimed at accurately measuring and collecting each employer’s share of unfunded vested benefits, and it requires the plan’s calculation to rest on actuarial assumptions that are “actuarially reasonable” and, in the aggregate, offer the actuary’s “best estimate” of anticipated experience (29 U.S.C. §§ 1381–1399, particularly § 1393). Nothing in § 1399(b)(1)’s “as soon as practicable” notice requirement or the arbitration channeling provisions suggests that an initial notice freezes an actuarial mistake into place where it would under-collect and shift costs onto remaining employers and ultimately threaten participants’ benefits—an outcome inconsistent with Congress’s protective design and PBGC’s role. Although § 1394(a) reflects Congress’s concern about retroactive rule changes that inflate liability after an employer withdraws, that anti-manipulation principle is satisfied here by requiring the revised assumptions to be actuarially reasonable and subject to arbitration review, rather than by forbidding any correction that improves accuracy. Metz is best read as expressing concern with retroactive inflation and predictability, but it does not compel a categorical bar on recalculation where the plan is correcting assumptions to conform to § 1393’s statutory standard rather than opportunistically changing policy.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: MPPAA’s withdrawal-liability scheme is built around a fixed “snapshot” of unfunded vested benefits as of the end of the plan year preceding withdrawal, with notice and collection triggered by the plan sponsor’s assessment under 29 U.S.C. §§ 1381–1383 and 1399, and disputes funneled into arbitration on a pay-now-dispute-later model that depends on administrable finality. While § 1393(a) requires actuarial assumptions to be “actuarially reasonable” and used “in combination” to determine UVBs, nothing in the text authorizes a plan to reopen a completed assessment to substitute a new interest-rate assumption simply because it later prefers (or adopts) a different rate; that kind of retroactive re-selection functions like an impermissible post-snapshot change and threatens workability by inviting repeated re-demands. Metz supports the principle that assumptions applicable as of the relevant measurement date control and that post hoc changes cannot be used to increase liability over an employer’s objection; any permissible “correction” is best limited to true computational/clerical mistakes rather than a discretionary change in a key assumption. Given MPPAA’s emphasis on predictability and the structured timing of § 1399 notices and arbitration, I would hold plans may not retroactively increase liability by changing actuarial assumptions after issuing the demand.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The MPPAA’s text establishes a sequenced, time-bound process: the plan must determine withdrawal liability based on unfunded vested benefits as of the measurement date and then issue notice and demand “as soon as practicable,” 29 U.S.C. §§ 1381, 1399(b)(1); it does not authorize a second, retroactive re-selection of core actuarial assumptions after an assessment has issued. Allowing trustees to reopen and increase liability by changing the interest-rate assumption would undermine the statute’s notice-and-arbitration scheme (with tight deadlines for the employer’s request for review and initiation of arbitration), §§ 1399(b)(2), 1401(a), by denying employers a stable, reviewable assessment to contest. The Second Circuit’s Metz decision is best read to impose a bright-line rule tying the calculation to the assumptions adopted on the valuation/measurement date, permitting only corrections of clerical or arithmetical mistakes rather than discretionary, outcome-changing assumption swaps. To the extent any ambiguity remains in a regime imposing substantial, mandatory payments, separation-of-powers and lenity-like concerns counsel against inferring a broad, unstated power in plans to retroactively ratchet liability upward.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: MPPAA’s withdrawal-liability scheme is built around predictable notice and a prompt arbitration process keyed to a defined “measurement date,” and allowing plans to retroactively swap in new actuarial assumptions after issuing an assessment would undermine finality and workability. The Second Circuit’s decision in Nat’l Ret. Fund v. Metz Culinary Mgmt., Inc., 946 F.3d 146 (2d Cir. 2020), draws a bright-line rule that the actuarial assumptions and methods in place on the measurement date must govern the calculation, rejecting a post hoc interest-rate change that dramatically increased liability. That approach is reinforced by Congress’s anti-manipulation concern in 29 U.S.C. § 1394(a), which bars retroactive plan-rule changes that inflate a withdrawing employer’s liability, and it fits the statute’s emphasis on restraint and administrable rules over after-the-fact discretion. Plans remain able to correct true clerical or arithmetic errors, but ERISA/MPPAA does not authorize materially increasing liability by retroactively re-selecting key actuarial assumptions after the assessment has been issued.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The MPPAA’s text ties withdrawal liability to an assessment that the plan must issue “as soon as practicable” after withdrawal, followed by a prompt dispute-resolution track culminating in arbitration, 29 U.S.C. §§ 1399(b)(1), 1401(a), which presupposes a determinate calculation rather than an open-ended power to increase liability later by reselecting key actuarial assumptions. Section 1393(a) requires “actuarially reasonable” assumptions, but it does not authorize retroactive substitution of a new interest rate after notice has issued; reading such authority in would undercut the finality and predictability that the notice/arbitration scheme is structured to provide. Metz (2d Cir.) is most consistent with that structure in drawing a line between correcting true calculation errors and retroactively changing discretionary assumptions after the valuation date to inflate liability. Precedent and methodological consistency therefore favor holding that recalculation to increase liability by changing assumptions post-assessment is not permitted under §§ 1381–1399 and § 1401(a).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: MPPAA ties the calculation of unfunded vested benefits to a fixed “measurement date”—“as of the end of the plan year preceding the plan year in which the employer withdraws,” 29 U.S.C. § 1391(b)(2)(E)(i)—and § 1399(b) then requires prompt “notice and demand,” a structure that serves finality and procedural fairness for the withdrawing employer. Allowing a plan to retroactively swap in a materially different interest-rate assumption after the measurement date (and after issuing an assessment) would undercut that statutory timing rule and invite strategic revisions inconsistent with predictable notice, even if disputes are channeled to arbitration under § 1401(a). The Second Circuit in Nat’l Ret. Fund v. Metz Culinary Mgmt., Inc. held that the relevant actuarial assumptions must be those in place by the end of the measurement date and rejected retroactive changes that inflate liability, and that bright-line approach best aligns with MPPAA’s procedural framework. Corrections for genuine clerical or arithmetical errors may be different, but discretionary re-selection of key assumptions post hoc is not what Congress contemplated when it fixed the measurement date and mandated prompt notice.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a multiemployer pension plan may retroactively revise the actuarial assumptions (especially the interest/discount rate) used to calculate an employer’s ERISA/MPPAA withdrawal liability after the employer has withdrawn, thereby increasing the assessed liability.
case_analysis.legal_provision: ERISA as amended by the Multiemployer Pension Plan Amendments Act of 1980 (MPPAA), primarily 29 U.S.C. §§ 1381–1405 (withdrawal liability calculation and allocation), and related provisions governing actuarial assumptions and plan determinations (including 29 U.S.C. §§ 1393 and 1401).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (M&K Employee Solutions and related parties) argue that once an employer’s withdrawal liability is triggered and calculated, the plan must use actuarial assumptions that are properly adopted and applicable as of the relevant valuation/measurement date, and it cannot later ‘true up’ the assessment by retroactively changing the interest-rate/discount-rate assumptions to produce a higher bill. They contend the Fund’s approach unlawfully rewrites the calculation after the fact, undermines predictability and the statutory pay-now-dispute-later framework, and conflicts with appellate authority (notably the Second Circuit’s decision in Metz) and arbitral decisions rejecting retroactive assumption changes as inconsistent with MPPAA’s structure and ERISA’s actuarial-assumptions requirements.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund), supported by the United States and labor/pension amici, argues that MPPAA requires withdrawal liability to reflect the plan’s actual unfunded vested benefits using reasonable actuarial assumptions; if a plan determines that the assumptions used in an initial assessment were erroneous, incomplete, or not in compliance with governing standards, the plan may correct the calculation—even if that means revising the interest/discount-rate assumption used—so that the assessed amount matches the liability mandated by statute. They emphasize administrative practicality, the need to protect plan funding and participants, and the statutory design that channels disputes into arbitration while allowing plans to collect interim payments, contending that prohibiting corrective recalculations would lock in understatements, shift costs to remaining employers and participants, and impair plan solvency.
key_precedents: Metz (Second Circuit) (cited for the proposition that plans cannot retroactively alter interest-rate assumptions used to calculate withdrawal liability)
Jacobson v. Fireman’s Fund Ins. Co., 111 F.3d 2d (2d Cir. 1997) (mentioned in the provided excerpt)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest argument is that § 1393(a)(1)’s “best estimate”/“reasonable in the aggregate” standard is substantive and, with Concrete Pipe’s presumption-of-correctness framework, implies room to revise an assessment that used an unreasonable discount rate. But that reading gives insufficient weight to the statute’s timing architecture that Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize: § 1399(b)(1) requires a prompt assessment keyed to “the assumptions used for the most recent actuarial valuation,” followed immediately by interim payments under § 1399(c) and dispute resolution in arbitration under § 1401—features that presuppose a fixed snapshot rather than a moving-target bill. Justice Alito’s reliance on § 1401(a)(3)(B)’s “significant error” language does not overcome that structure; consistent with Metz, I read it to permit correction of computational or misapplication errors within the valuation-year assumption set, not a retroactive substitution of a core actuarial judgment like the discount rate that predictably ratchets liability upward after withdrawal. A narrow holding barring post-withdrawal changes to the governing actuarial assumptions (while allowing correction of clerical/method-application mistakes and prospective changes) best fits the text, preserves administrability, and protects institutional legitimacy in the pay-now-dispute-later regime.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest argument—that § 1393(a)(1)’s “best estimate” and “reasonable” requirements are substantive and therefore should allow later revisions to cure an unreasonable assumption—does not overcome the statute’s textual time anchor: § 1399(b)(1) directs use of “the assumptions used for the most recent actuarial valuation,” and § 1393(b) frames reasonableness by reference to assumptions “in the plan year in which the liability was incurred.” Justice Alito’s reliance on § 1401(a)(3)(B) and Concrete Pipe is not to the contrary, because “significant error” is best read (as the Chief Justice and Justice Gorsuch suggest) to permit correction of misapplication or computational mistakes within the governing valuation snapshot, not retroactive substitution of a new discount-rate judgment that reopens the valuation itself. Concrete Pipe’s presumption-of-correctness regime presumes correctness of determinations made under the statute’s rules; it cannot supply an unstated power to ratchet liability upward after withdrawal where the text instead emphasizes prompt determination, interim payments, and arbitration as the avenue to test the reasonableness of the valuation-date assumptions. Under an original public meaning approach, Congress would have spoken clearly if it intended to authorize post-withdrawal assumption “do-overs” that increase liability in a scheme otherwise designed to be swift, settled, and administrable.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s administrability and reliance concerns (and Justice Thomas’s timing “snapshot” reading of § 1399(b)(1)) are the strongest points for Petitioner, but they still do not supply a clear textual bar on correcting a concededly mistaken discount-rate application. Section 1401(a)(3)(B)’s express direction to correct “significant error[s]” in applying assumptions is difficult to reconcile with Petitioner’s categorical no-revision rule; if Congress meant “significant error” to exclude correction of a demonstrably misapplied actuarial assumption, it could have said so. I agree with Justice Kagan that Concrete Pipe’s presumption-of-correctness framework, coupled with arbitration review for unreasonableness or misapplication, is the statute’s chosen safeguard against opportunistic “ratcheting,” making an extra-textual freeze unnecessary. Metz’s bright-line rule has practical appeal, but as Justice Roberts’s reading illustrates, it depends more on inferred structure than on the statute’s words, and it risks entrenching noncompliant valuations contrary to § 1393’s command that liabilities reflect reasonable, properly applied assumptions.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest argument—that § 1393(a)’s “best estimate” is a substantive command and arbitration can police opportunistic revisions—does not overcome the scheme Congress actually designed: § 1399(b)’s prompt assessment and interim-payment regime depends on a settled, valuation-year snapshot so employers (and, downstream, workers whose jobs and benefits ride on the employer’s viability) are not subjected to a coercive moving-target bill. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh that reading § 1401(a)(3)(B)’s “significant error” language to permit retroactively swapping a core actuarial judgment like the discount rate would destabilize reliance and invite strategic “corrections,” effectively converting pay-now-dispute-later into pay-now-and-maybe-pay-more-later. Concrete Pipe’s presumption of correctness, as Justice Alito invokes it, cuts the other way for me: it presumes correctness of the determination made under the statute’s timing rules, with arbitration as the vehicle to challenge whether the valuation-date assumptions were reasonable—not a license for post-withdrawal do-overs that ratchet liability upward. On pragmatic fairness and access-to-justice grounds, the Metz-style measurement-date rule better protects administrability and prevents interim payments from becoming leverage against withdrawing employers in a way that can harm workers and smaller entities least able to absorb uncertainty.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s strongest point is structural: § 1399(b)’s prompt demand and interim payments work best if the assessment is a stable snapshot. But I don’t see in § 1399(b)(1)’s “assumptions used for the most recent actuarial valuation” an anti-correction command that overrides § 1393(a)(1)’s substantive requirement that the assumptions be the actuary’s best estimate and reasonable in the aggregate for that valuation; it identifies the valuation framework, not irrevocability. Justice Alito’s reliance on § 1401(a)(3)(B)’s “significant error” language and Concrete Pipe matters here because it confirms Congress anticipated corrections and then policing of reasonableness/misapplication in arbitration, which is a more textually coherent way to manage predictability concerns than reading in a categorical bar on revising an assumption later discovered not to reflect the actuary’s best estimate. The administrability and fairness worries raised by Justice Sotomayor are real, but under a pragmatic textualist approach they are addressed by limiting revisions to genuine error correction subject to arbitral review for bad faith or opportunistic ratcheting, rather than freezing in place a conceded statutory noncompliance.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Alito press the best argument for Respondent: § 1393(a)’s “best estimate/reasonable” requirements are substantive, and § 1401(a)(3)(B) contemplates correcting “significant error[s],” so a concededly mistaken discount rate should be fixable. But reading those provisions in context with § 1399(b)(1)’s directive to calculate using “the assumptions used for the most recent actuarial valuation” and § 1393(b)’s focus on assumptions “in the plan year in which the liability was incurred” yields a timing-anchored snapshot; “significant error” is naturally understood as misapplication or computation within that snapshot, not a post-withdrawal substitution of the actuary’s core valuation judgment. Chief Justice Roberts’s structural point about the pay-now-dispute-later regime is therefore dispositive for me: absent clear congressional authorization, we should not infer a rolling true-up power that destabilizes the demanded schedule and invites strategic ratcheting. Concrete Pipe’s presumption-of-correctness framework fits this view because it presumes correctness for the plan’s determination made under the statute’s fixed measurement rules, with arbitration to test reasonableness—not to reopen and replace the assumption set after the fact.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Alito press the best textual point: § 1393(a)’s “best estimate” and § 1401(a)(3)(B)’s “significant error” language imply some ability to correct mistakes, reinforced by Concrete Pipe’s presumption-of-correctness framework. But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, the statute’s architecture—§ 1399(b)’s prompt “determination” and schedule, § 1399(c)’s interim-payments regime, and § 1401’s channeling of disputes into arbitration—functions only if the assessment is a timing-anchored snapshot using the most recent valuation-year assumptions, with “corrections” confined to misapplication/clerical/computational errors rather than retroactively replacing a core actuarial judgment like the discount rate to increase liability. Concrete Pipe’s deference to the plan’s determination presumes a determination made under the statute’s timing rules; it does not supply affirmative authorization for post-withdrawal assumption substitutions that destabilize reliance and invite strategic ratcheting. Under my institutionalist approach, absent clear congressional authorization to reopen the assumption set after withdrawal, I read §§ 1393/1399/1401 together to preserve administrability and predictability while leaving the reasonableness of the original valuation assumptions to arbitration review.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan presses the best textual point for Respondent: § 1393(a)(1)’s “best estimate” and “reasonable” standards are substantive and should not freeze an acknowledged mistake. But read in context, § 1399(b)(1) directs the plan to “determine” liability using “the assumptions used for the most recent actuarial valuation,” and § 1393(b) asks whether the assumptions for the plan year in which liability was incurred were reasonable—language that, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, anchors the inquiry to a valuation-year snapshot rather than authorizing retroactive substitution of a new discount-rate judgment after withdrawal. Justice Alito’s reliance on § 1401(a)(3)(B) and Concrete Pipe does not move me because “correct[ing]” a “significant error” is most naturally read to mean correcting misapplication or computation within the governing valuation framework, not reopening the core actuarial selection itself in a way that destabilizes the statute’s prompt-notice/pay-now-dispute-later architecture. On an original public-meaning, textualist reading, Congress would have spoken clearly if it intended to permit post-withdrawal, upward “do-overs” of key actuarial assumptions, leaving arbitration to test the reasonableness of the snapshot assumptions rather than enabling later replacement.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s best argument is that § 1393(a)’s “best estimate” and “reasonable in the aggregate” requirements are substantive, so a plan shouldn’t be stuck with an assumption later recognized as noncompliant; Justice Alito reinforces this with § 1401(a)(3)(B)’s “significant error” language. But Chief Justice Roberts is right that the statute’s pay-now-dispute-later architecture in § 1399(b) and interim-payment mechanism in § 1399(c) depend on a fixed, prompt assessment keyed to the “most recent actuarial valuation,” with arbitration serving as the fairness check on whether those valuation-year assumptions were reasonable—not a license for a post-withdrawal ratchet via swapping a core actuarial judgment like the discount rate. Reading “significant error” to include retroactive replacement of the assumption set would, as Justice Sotomayor stresses, create a moving-target liability that is practically coercive and procedurally unfair given the statutory compulsion to pay while disputing. Concrete Pipe’s presumption-of-correctness fits better with a snapshot rule: it defers (subject to arbitration) to the plan’s determination made under the governing valuation framework, not to a rolling authority to redo that framework after withdrawal to increase liability.

John Roberts.reasoning: The MPPAA’s structure ties withdrawal liability to a determination made "as soon as practicable" after withdrawal, with disputes funneled into arbitration under § 1401 and interim payments required under § 1399(c); allowing retroactive changes to core assumptions after assessment undermines predictability and the pay-now-dispute-later framework. Section 1393(a) requires the plan’s actuary to use assumptions and methods that, in the aggregate, are reasonable and represent the actuary’s best estimate for the valuation, which points to fixing the relevant assumptions as of the measurement/valuation date rather than permitting later “true-ups” that increase a bill post-withdrawal. The Second Circuit’s rule in National Retirement Fund v. Metz Culinary Management, Inc. better fits that statutory design by preventing ex post revision of the discount rate to inflate liability, while still leaving plans room to select reasonable assumptions prospectively and to correct clerical errors through arbitration without reopening the substantive actuarial judgment. A narrow holding barring retroactive assumption changes (as distinct from correcting arithmetic mistakes) preserves uniformity and institutional legitimacy by providing a clear, administrable rule grounded in the statute’s timing and dispute-resolution provisions.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text and structure of the MPPAA anchor withdrawal liability to determinations made using settled assumptions at the relevant valuation/measurement point: § 1399(b)(1) directs the plan to compute and demand liability using "the assumptions used for the most recent actuarial valuation," and § 1393(a) requires "reasonable" assumptions chosen in advance for that valuation rather than revised after an employer exits. Nothing in §§ 1381–1405 authorizes trustees to reopen a completed assessment by retroactively changing the discount rate to increase the bill, and the limited instances where Congress expressly permitted post-withdrawal changes (e.g., § 1394’s treatment of certain retroactive plan amendments and related timing safeguards) underscore the absence of such authority for actuarial assumption do-overs. A contrary rule would expand plan power beyond the statute’s original public meaning and undermine the predictable, rule-bound scheme Congress enacted, leaving employers subject to after-the-fact liability increases untethered to the measurement-date assumptions. Metz best reflects this statutory timing constraint and the principle that retroactive increases require clear congressional authorization.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The statutory text directs that withdrawal liability reflect the plan’s “unfunded vested benefits” as determined using actuarial assumptions that are reasonable in the aggregate and properly applied, and § 1401(a)(3)(B) expressly contemplates correcting “significant error[s]” in applying assumptions; nothing in §§ 1381–1405 freezes an initially used discount rate if the plan later determines it was erroneous or noncompliant. Concrete Pipe confirms Congress placed primary responsibility for these determinations on the plan sponsor and its actuary, with a presumption of correctness in arbitration and judicial review focused on whether assumptions/methods were unreasonable in the aggregate or misapplied. As a practical matter consistent with MPPAA’s pay-now-dispute-later design, allowing corrective recalculations protects plan solvency and avoids shifting understatements to remaining employers and participants. While Metz suggests limits on retroactive changes, I would not extend it to bar good-faith corrections necessary to align the assessment with the liability mandated by statute.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: MPPAA’s pay-now-dispute-later regime in 29 U.S.C. § 1401 depends on administrable, predictable assessments tied to the plan’s valuation/measurement date, and ERISA requires actuarial assumptions to be reasonable and applied consistently for that determination, see 29 U.S.C. § 1393. Allowing a plan to retroactively change the discount/interest-rate assumption after withdrawal to increase the bill undermines fairness and access to justice by imposing shifting, unforeseeable liabilities on withdrawing employers and their workers, and invites strategic recalculation rather than timely, transparent adoption of assumptions. The Second Circuit’s rule in National Retirement Fund v. Metz—requiring interest-rate assumptions to be determined as of the measurement date, with prior-year assumptions rolling over absent a timely change—best fits the statute’s structure and protects against after-the-fact ratcheting of liability. While protecting plan solvency is important, ERISA provides mechanisms to adopt and apply proper assumptions prospectively and to resolve disputes in arbitration without permitting retroactive assumption changes that destabilize settled assessments.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The text of § 1393(a)(1) directs that the actuarial assumptions used to determine withdrawal liability be, in the aggregate, “reasonable” and, in combination, the actuary’s “best estimate” of anticipated experience; that standard is substantive, not a one-time procedural freeze at the moment a § 1399(b)(1) notice issues. Read with § 1401’s pay-now-dispute-later arbitration scheme and the presumption of correctness recognized in Concrete Pipe, the statute is workable only if a plan may correct an assessment when it discovers that the assumptions applied were not the actuary’s best estimate or were otherwise unreasonable—subject to arbitral/judicial review for manipulation or bad faith. Metz’s categorical bar on post-withdrawal assumption revisions is not compelled by the statutory language and risks locking in acknowledged errors and shifting unfunded vested benefits onto remaining employers and participants, contrary to MPPAA’s allocation design in §§ 1381–1405. The better middle-ground rule is that revisions are permissible only to bring the determination into compliance with § 1393(a)(1)’s reasonableness/best-estimate requirements, not to opportunistically inflate liability.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The MPPAA’s text directs that withdrawal liability be determined based on the plan’s unfunded vested benefits as of the statutory measurement date, using actuarial assumptions and methods that, under 29 U.S.C. § 1393(a), represent the actuary’s “best estimate” and are “reasonable” in the aggregate at that time—not later assumptions adopted after withdrawal to increase a specific employer’s bill. Allowing a plan to retroactively revise the discount rate after the employer withdraws effectively rewrites the completed statutory calculation in §§ 1381–1391, undermining the statute’s pay-now-dispute-later framework in § 1401 by converting a fixed assessment into a moving target. The Second Circuit’s Metz rule supplies a bright-line, text-consistent timing principle: the assumptions in place on the measurement date govern, and retroactive assumption changes to inflate liability are impermissible. Any ambiguity about timing should be resolved against after-the-fact liability expansion, consistent with predictability and the separation-of-powers concern that courts should not create a roving equitable “true up” power absent clear statutory authorization.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: MPPAA’s structure and timing provisions point to using the actuarial assumptions “in effect” for the applicable plan year/measurement date, rather than permitting a plan to retroactively change a key assumption after withdrawal to increase the bill. Section 1393(a) requires withdrawal liability to be determined on the basis of “actuarial assumptions and methods which, in the aggregate, are reasonable” and—critically—§ 1393(b) ties that reasonableness inquiry to the plan’s assumptions “in the plan year in which the liability was incurred,” while § 1399(b) contemplates a prompt post-withdrawal “determination” and payment schedule that would be destabilized if plans could later re-rate the discount assumption to inflate liability. The Second Circuit’s Metz decision supplies a workable bright-line rule consistent with predictability, reliance, and the pay-now-dispute-later system: use the assumptions applicable as of the statutory measurement date, and correct only calculation errors within that framework rather than retroactively adopting new assumptions to increase liability. Allowing retroactive assumption revisions would invite after-the-fact manipulation and undermine the statute’s practical administrability and legitimacy-driven need for clear, settled rules.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The MPPAA’s text contemplates a “snapshot” calculation keyed to the plan year and the valuation/measurement date, with actuarial assumptions supplied under 29 U.S.C. § 1393 and then a demand-and-review/arbitration sequence under §§ 1399–1401; that structure presupposes that the assumptions “in effect” for the pertinent valuation govern the assessment, subject to dispute over their reasonableness—not later replacement. Allowing a plan to retroactively revise the discount rate after withdrawal to increase liability functions like an impermissible post hoc change to the rules governing the assessment and undermines the predictability Congress built into the pay-now-dispute-later regime. Precedent such as Metz (2d Cir.) supports this reading by rejecting retroactive application of a changed interest-rate assumption to a prior measurement year and pointing to statutory indications (including § 1394(a)’s anti-retroactivity principle) that post-snapshot changes should not be used to increase an employer’s liability over its objection. The Fund’s solvency and “correction” arguments may be weighty as policy, but the better textual fit is that any correction must occur within the statutory process using the assumptions applicable to the relevant measurement date, with reasonableness tested in arbitration under § 1401.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: MPPAA’s withdrawal-liability scheme fixes the calculation to a defined measurement date and channels disputes into arbitration under a pay-now-dispute-later framework, which depends on predictable, procedurally fair assessments rather than after-the-fact upward “true ups.” Reading 29 U.S.C. §§ 1381–1405 and § 1391 alongside § 1393’s requirement that assumptions be “reasonable” and represent “the actuary’s best estimate,” the better interpretation is that the plan must apply the properly adopted assumptions applicable as of the relevant valuation/measurement date, not retroactively revise key inputs like the discount rate after withdrawal to increase the bill. The Second Circuit’s decision in National Retirement Fund v. Metz supports that statutory structure by rejecting retroactive post-measurement-date assumption changes, and that approach avoids unfair surprise and protects reliance interests critical to orderly employer exits. While plan solvency is important, Congress provided tools (including interim payments and arbitration) that do not require reopening the core assumptions after withdrawal in a way that undermines uniform, procedurally fair administration.
